query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of 2 at.% Al to Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance without sacrificing its useful mechanical performance.
generation.structural_mediator: formation of a protective Al2O3 layer
generation.boundary: temperature: 1000 °C, atmosphere: air, exposure time: 100 hours, mechanical-loading: 10^-4 - 10^-2 s^-1
generation.uncertainty: The actual improvement in oxidation resistance may vary depending on the specific processing conditions and microstructure of the alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: oxidation test at 1000 °C in air for 100 hours
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the weight gain is less than 10% and the microstructure shows no significant degradation, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: This dynamic oxygen embrittlement behavior has been reported in several other superalloys and intermetal complexes at a similar temperature range, which greatly limits their practical applications []. However, only a small number of impurities formed due to oxidation were found upon the fracture, which were not observed in either SEM or TEM observations. This indicates that the oxidative effect was not severe. Second, it may be due to a precipitation at high temperatures. The significant decrease in ductility at 1073 K is similar to that found in the TiZrHfNbTa alloy []. The precipitates from the grain boundary can damage the plasticity of the alloy. However, a previous analysis showed that the alloy had a single-phase BCC structure, and no precipitation was found by TEM. The possible reason is that the size of these precipitates was small, only a few nanometers in size, and it took a considerable time to find them in the field of view of TEM. This phenomenon will be the subject of another study. There are some researches working on the addition of Al [,], Mo [], Ti [], V [], or Zr [], but few of them focus on the elevated-temperature mechanical performance and the overall effect of the constituent elements. To understand the elemental effect on mechanical properties, equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy is firstly designed as a base alloy by adding the high modulus refractory element Mo to HfNbTaTiZr. Then the subtraction method is used to analyze each elemental effect in the equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr. Thus, in this study, six alloys HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi are investigated and compared on their microstructure. Further, the compressive properties at room temperature and at elevated temperature are investigated. By comparing HfMoNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr, the influence of the addition of Mo can be understood. Likewise, the influence of the addition of Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr can be articulated. In addition, promising compositions were found and further improved design is suggested. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solid solution strengthening effect will be discussed.
